title: A protocol's risk rating shifts the exposure-tolerance window rather than scaling the capital charge
content:
The reference implementation of the smart-contract piecewise function makes explicit what the prose formulas at A.3.2.2.1.2.3.3.1.5.1–.3 state only symbolically:

```
x_start = (50 - rating) * 0.01
x_max   = x_start + 0.50   # always a 50% gap to max
x_kink  = x_start + 0.75 * (x_max - x_start)
```

The curve's *shape* never changes. Its width is always 50 percentage points, the kink always sits three quarters of the way across, and the output always runs 0% → 25% → 100%. The only thing the risk rating does is **translate the window horizontally**.

That is a materially different design from scaling a charge by riskiness. A rating of 0 puts `x_start` at 50%, so the ecosystem can be exposed up to half of total system debt before any smart-contract capital is required at all. A rating of 50 puts `x_start` at 0, so the very first unit of exposure attracts a charge. Between those, each rating point costs one percentage point of free allowance.

So the framework's claim is that safety is best expressed as *how much you may hold before capital is required*, not as *how much capital per unit held*. Below the start threshold the requirement is exactly zero — the docstring confirms "0% coverage if x < x_start" — which means well-rated protocols are genuinely free to use at moderate scale, and the capital regime only engages once concentration reaches a rating-dependent point.

The consequence is a sharp gradient once engaged. Because the width is fixed at 50 points regardless of rating, crossing `x_start` starts the same climb to 100% for every protocol; a good rating delays the onset but does not soften the slope. Combined with the kink at 75% of the span mapping to only 25% coverage, most of the capital burden is concentrated in the final quarter of the window — mild through the approach, then steep.
description: Thresholds are x_start = (50 − rating) × 1%, width always 50 points, kink always at 75% — so a better rating buys a larger zero-capital allowance, not a discount on the same curve.
